analysis.one_liner: Bars insurers from charging more out-of-pocket for breast cancer diagnostic tests than for screenings.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with support from one Republican and one Democratic senator, never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Affordable Care Act, most plans must cover routine breast cancer screening mammograms with no cost to the patient. But when a screening finds something abnormal and the doctor orders a diagnostic exam, extra mammogram images, an ultrasound, or an MRI, many plans treat that as a different service and charge deductibles, coinsurance, or copays. This bill would require plans to apply the same cost-sharing and limits to diagnostic exams as they do to screenings, and it would forbid insurers from dodging the rule by raising charges on screenings instead. It also applies to plans that previously were exempt from such requirements.
analysis.who_benefits: Women whose screening mammograms show an abnormality and who then need diagnostic imaging. They would no longer face surprise bills of hundreds of dollars at the moment they are anxiously waiting to learn whether they have cancer. Earlier, more affordable follow-up testing can catch cancers sooner, when treatment is cheaper and more effective.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to apply cost-sharing and treatment limits to diagnostic breast exams (mammography, ultrasound, MRI) that are no worse than those applied to screening exams [S2] [S3].
Blocks insurers from complying simply by adding new charges to routine screening mammograms instead [S3].
Extends the rule to grandfathered health plans that are otherwise exempt from many new insurance requirements, effective for plan years starting January 1, 2022 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would absorb the cost of diagnostic imaging they currently shift to patients through deductibles and copays, and those costs would likely be spread into premiums. Insurers would keep the ability to require prior authorization and other utilization controls, which limits how open-ended the cost is.

drawbacks.text: The added coverage would raise premiums somewhat for everyone enrolled in a plan, including people who never need breast imaging [S3].

The bill does not eliminate cost-sharing for diagnostic exams outright; a plan that charges for screenings could still charge the same for diagnostics, so patients in high-deductible plans would still pay [S3].
Plans retain the right to require prior authorization before approving imaging, which can still delay follow-up care [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and real: a woman whose screening shows something abnormal should not face a surprise bill for the tests that determine whether it is cancer. The cost is a modest premium increase spread across all enrollees, softened by the bill leaving insurers' prior-authorization tools intact and not mandating zero cost-sharing. On balance a reasonable, narrow patient-protection bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health Committee, where no action was ever taken on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 12, 2021 by Senator Roy Blunt with Senator Jeanne Shaheen [S1] [S3].
Read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history before the 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers keep charging deductibles and copays on diagnostic breast imaging, the follow-up tests women need after an abnormal screening, since no comparable federal rule was enacted in that Congress. Women facing diagnostic follow-ups continue to bear those out-of-pocket costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers keep diagnostic imaging charges

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with a Democratic cosponsor, and no vote was ever taken, so no party split shows up in the record.

industries.note: Plans currently charge deductibles, coinsurance, or copays on diagnostic mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs even when screenings are covered free. The bill would force them to absorb those costs or fold them into premiums.
Removing out-of-pocket barriers makes patients more likely to complete recommended follow-up imaging, which benefits imaging practices and, ideally, catches cancers earlier.
